rules.quote: Capitalise the titles of the current prime minister and treasurer
rules.specification: Interpret the capitalisation instruction as applying to titles identifying particular current office holders, not to generic role descriptions such as the lower-case plurals in the list of parliamentary website links. The explicit lower-case instructions for generic and former office holders concern prime ministers and treasurers.
rules.violation_condition: An official title identifying a current Australian parliamentary office holder is incorrectly lower-cased, or ‘prime minister’ or ‘treasurer’ is capitalised when used generically or for a former Australian office holder.
when: Capitalise the titles of the current Australian Prime Minister and Treasurer, including abbreviated forms.
Use lower case for generic references to prime ministers and treasurers.
Use lower case for former Australian prime ministers and treasurers.
Capitalise titles identifying current senators and members of the Australian Parliament.
rules.why: G-2 combines office-holder and generic-reference conditions for the same capitalisation check; G-4 avoids duplicate heading and body rules.

when: Federal ministers, including the prime minister, and parliamentary secretaries receive the title and retain it for life.
The federal examples also illustrate serving and former assistant ministers.
The President of the Senate and Speaker of the House of Representatives receive the title.
Federal parliamentarians who are former state ministers or former presiding officers of state parliaments receive the title.

rules.specification: Determine recipient role and formal or less formal correspondence from document context or supplied metadata. Do not invent a linguistic threshold for formality.
rules.violation_condition: Correspondence to one of the specified office holders lacks the opening appropriate to the recipient’s office and the stated level of formality.
when: For a federal minister, use Dear Minister in formal emails and letters and My dear Minister in less formal correspondence.
For an ordinary state or territory parliamentarian, use Dear with the applicable personal title, such as Ms, Mr, Mrs, Mx or Dr, in formal and less formal correspondence.
For a state premier, use Dear Premier formally and My dear Premier less formally.
For either territory chief minister, use Dear Chief Minister in formal and less formal correspondence.
For a capital-city lord mayor, use Dear Lord Mayor.
For other mayors, use Dear Mayor, or Dear Lord Mayor where applicable.
For a shire president, alderman or councillor in formal emails and letters, use Dear President, Dear Alderman or Dear Councillor as appropriate.
For less formal correspondence to those local office holders, the specified openings are Dear President, Dear Alderman or Dear Councillor followed by the family name in the councillor form.
Apply office-specific openings in preference to the general state-or-territory-member opening.
rules.why: G-2 makes recipient office and formality conditions of one correspondence-opening check rather than separate overlapping salutation rules.

rules.specification: Determine formal or less formal correspondence from document context or supplied metadata, rather than inventing a textual threshold.
rules.violation_condition: Correspondence to one of the specified office holders lacks the prescribed closing for its recipient category and level of formality.
when: For federal ministers, state and territory parliamentarians, state premiers, territory chief ministers, shire presidents, aldermen and councillors, use Yours faithfully in formal correspondence and Yours sincerely in less formal correspondence.
For lord mayors and other mayors, use Yours faithfully; the page supplies no less-formal alternative.
rules.why: G-2 consolidates repeated closing instructions and their formality conditions; opening and closing remain distinct findings.
